summary: An inferential framework for multi-LLM routing. It separates outcome-oracle opportunity (run every model, pick a correct one) from signal-restricted and learned-router gain, and gives exact Clopper-Pearson style intervals that stay valid after selecting the empirical best model or the best member of a router family. A confirmatory run uses eight open checkpoints (0.5-7B) on ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, GSM8K and MMLU (200-300 test items each). The oracle gap is certified positive on all four tasks (point estimates 9.7-30.7 pp). The best K-way pre-answer router recovers 7.5-14.4% of it, and the simultaneous interval for the best of 11 policies over the best fixed model has lower limit exactly zero on every task.

claims.claim: The oracle routing opportunity is a real population property, not an artifact of same-sample best-model selection
claims.evidence: Table 1: selection-valid 95% lower limits .016/.162/.041/.181 on ARC-C/HellaSwag/GSM8K/MMLU, positive after a Bonferroni budget over K=8. 50/50 calibration/test split with the test half opened once. The positive certificate is about 1.6-18.1 pp, not the 9.7-30.7 pp point estimates.

claims.claim: Tested pre-answer routers recover only 7.5-14.4% of the certified opportunity
claims.evidence: Table 3: best deployable K-way router gain .014/.026/.015/.023 over the frozen task-wise best model. The fractions divide point-estimate gains by point-estimate gaps; no interval is given for the fraction itself. The routers are uniform K-way adaptations of published mechanisms, not the authors' released systems (§9).

claims.claim: After selection among 11 policies the data do not certify that any router beats the best fixed model, while opportunity beyond the family is certified
claims.evidence: Table 2: G_Pi lower limit .000 on all four datasets; H_Pi lower limits .011-.175. Follows from Theorem 6 with the failure budget split three ways. A lower limit of zero is absence of certified gain, not evidence of no gain.

claims.claim: Greedy complementary coverage is near-optimal for pool construction but coverage does not convert into router gain
claims.evidence: Appendix J: 1,120-cell sweep, greedy reaches 0.849-1.000 of exhaustive optimum (mean .997); held-out coverage usually inside random-subset p05-p95.

claims.claim: Cost-aware routers buy a small gain at 62-78% of reference cost, far below the cost-aware oracle
claims.evidence: Appendix H summary only in main text; same small-model pool and datasets.

patterns.note: Pre-answer K-way model routing does not certifiably beat the best fixed model on four single-turn benchmarks with a 0.5-7B pool, although complementary correct answers exist. Not agentic and not hosted frontier models.
Cost-aware routing extension (Appendix C/H) shows small gains at 62-78% of reference cost; no agent token budgets.
Contributes an evaluation method (selection-valid intervals, held-out G_learn) applicable to router or harness comparisons; uses no SWE-bench data.

methodology.sample: ARC-Challenge 300, HellaSwag 300, GSM8K 200, MMLU 300 (stratified over 57 subjects), plus code pass@1 and factual QA at 500 each; 50/50 calibration/test split, five-fold cross-fitting for routers
methodology.baselines: Eight fixed models, task-wise best fixed model, prompt routers, K-way adaptations of RouterDC, EmbedLLM, MODEL-SAT, GraphRouter, Avengers, Zooter, IRT-Router, fine-tuned K-head encoder, cost-aware and binary methods, post-inference selectors, nondeployable oracles
methodology.models: TinyLlama-1.1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B, Phi-3.5-mini, Mistral-7B (pinned revisions)
methodology.variance: Exact Clopper-Pearson intervals with selection-valid Bonferroni budgets; paired McNemar contrasts; greedy decoding, single generation per item
methodology.ablations: Pilot (4 models) vs confirmatory (8 models); signal classes; pool-construction sweep; post-inference selectors
methodology.contamination_controls: None reported; public benchmarks with small open models
methodology.languages: English; one code-generation setting, no repository tasks

standards.artifacts: Artifact and single-script provenance described (Appendix F); no repository URL found in the text
standards.preregistration: Predeclared confirmatory design with a held-out test half opened once (Appendix D); not externally registered

biases.detail: Single-turn multiple-choice and arithmetic benchmarks; no multi-turn or agentic coding tasks.
200-300 test items per dataset; the authors concede per-dataset intervals are wide and only certificate-level claims are firm.
All eight models are 0.5-7B open checkpoints. Cheap-versus-frontier routing among hosted models is not tested, so recovered fractions may differ when capability gaps are large.
Routers are uniform K-way re-implementations of published mechanisms, not authors' released systems; the paper flags this itself.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Open-weight checkpoints only; no product promoted
coi.detail: Academic authors, no vendor affiliation, negative result about routing products in general.

verdict_reason: The inferential method is careful: held-out test half, cross-fitting, exact post-selection intervals, and a negative result stated as a certificate. The evidence comes from small open models on single-turn benchmarks, so it says little about routing between a cheap and a frontier coding agent.
applicability: For a Java team the transferable part is the evaluation discipline, not the numbers. Before adding a cheap-vs-expensive model router or an agent cascade, measure the oracle gap on held-out tasks, report the learned router's held-out gain with a selection-valid interval, and compare it to the best single model. The paper does not show that coding-agent routing fails.

conflicts_with.detail: ACRouter reports online feedback-driven routing beating static routers and Always-Opus on cost-aware regret for coding tasks; this paper finds pre-answer routers do not certifiably beat the best fixed model. Different settings (online with feedback vs pre-answer; coding vs MCQ) limit the conflict.

UniScale reports joint routing plus test-time compute beating either alone on single-turn math without selection-valid intervals; this paper's Proposition 3 predicts such plug-in comparisons are biased upward.
